steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our survey on deep generative models in the retail supply chain. Cover the rise of generative AI, the phases and challenges of the retail supply chain, how existing surveys fall short, and our contributions and paper structure.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Rise of generative AI and deep generative models (DGMs)
2. The retail supply chain and its three phases
3. Challenges in each phase
4. Existing surveys and their gaps
5. Our contributions and paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Generative AI
- rapid advance of AI, blossoming of generative models -> new era; changes how we perceive, interact, innovate with technology
- ChatGPT, DALL-E: power of generating text/images
- human-like text, understanding context, artistic content -> revolutionary; attention to science behind it: Deep Generative Models (DGMs)
- practitioners leveraging DGMs in healthcare, finance, entertainment, etc.

2. Retail supply chain
- key component of modern economy; smooth flow of goods origin -> end-users
- three phases: purchase, logistics, sell
- purchase: strategic acquisition from vendors; driven by demand forecasting, procurement policies
- logistics: vendors -> distribution centers (DCs) -> retail outlets; vital for efficiency/effectiveness
- sell: sale + delivery to customers; completes cycle supplier -> consumer

3. Challenges
- complexity -> challenges in each phase
- demand forecasting: long-existing challenge in purchase; unpredictable consumer behavior, market conditions
- modeling/simulating supply chain to anticipate disruptions, bottlenecks; many variables + stochastic elements -> advanced tools
- optimality gap: theoretical best vs real-world execution; causes: logistical stochasticity, end-to-end visibility, computational NP-hardness
- inefficiencies ripple: delayed deliveries, increased carrying costs, diminished service levels -> value in methods improving optimality
- adapt/optimize end-to-end = survival imperative in global commerce

4. Existing surveys
- Ooi et al: potentials of DGMs across disciplines incl. retail; timely, high-level, many areas' supply chains, not retail-focused
- similar survey elsewhere
- article on ChatGPT etc. as game changer for 21st century supply chain excellence; specific applications, mainly language models, not techniques in retail
- review of 43 papers: deep learning in supply chain management, trends, perspectives, gaps; not exclusively DGMs or retail
- survey of DGMs (Energy-based models, VAEs, GANs, Autoregressive models) + supply chain applications; not end-to-end; not retail; no insights on specific retail problems

5. Contributions / organization
- no existing survey on DGMs in retail supply chain -> fill gap: techniques + business usecases
- (1) taxonomy, overview of state-of-the-art DGMs and variants
- (2) review of DGM applications in retail supply chain, end-to-end view
- (3) insights, potential directions
- Sec 2 DGM overview/taxonomy; Sec 3 purchase; Sec 4 logistics; Sec 5 sell; Sec 6 summary/conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Artificial intelligence is advancing fast, and in particular generative models are blossoming, which has started a new era for many fields and changed the way we perceive, interact and innovate with technology. Tools like ChatGPT and DALL-E show the world how powerful they are at generating content like text or images.

Their ability to generate human-like text, to understand context and even to create artistic content was revolutionary, and it brought people's attention to the science behind these AI tools, which is Deep Generative Models (DGMs). Practitioners are trying to use DGMs to pivot their areas, which are as diverse as healthcare, finance, entertainment and more, and they are doing it in a storming way.

The retail supply chain is a key part of the modern economy and it makes sure goods flow smoothly from their origin to end-users. In general it can be split into three phases: purchase, logistics, and sell. In the purchase phase, goods are acquired strategically from vendors, and this is driven by demand forecasting and procurement policies. Logistics is the second phase and it is about transporting these goods from vendors to distribution centers (DCs), and then from DCs to retail outlets. This step is vital for keeping the supply chain efficient and effective. The last phase is sell, which is the actual sale and then the delivery of products to customers, and this completes the cycle from supplier to consumer.

Because the modern retail supply chain is so complex, many challenges come up in each phase, and this motivates researchers and practitioners to look for innovative solutions. For example, forecasting demand accurately is a long-existing challenge in the purchase phase, and it is often fraught with the unpredictability of consumer behavior and market conditions. On top of this, the supply chain has to be modeled and simulated to anticipate potential disruptions and bottlenecks. Creating accurate models is complex because there are many variables and stochastic elements in supply chain processes, and this needs advanced tools and methodologies. Another example is the optimality gap, which is the difference between the most efficient theoretical solution and the real-world execution, and it is a persistent issue. This gap can come from different factors, including but not limited to logistical stochasticity, supply chain end-to-end visibility, and computational NP-hardness. These discrepancies often cause inefficiencies that ripple through the supply chain and show up as delayed deliveries, increased carrying costs, and diminished service levels, so it is always impactful and valuable to develop advanced methods that improve optimality. So being able to adapt and optimize the end-to-end process is not just a competitive advantage but a survival imperative in the volatile landscape of global commerce.

- existing surveys of DGMs in supply chain:
  - Ooi et al: DGM potentials across disciplines incl. retail; timely, insightful, but high-level, many areas' supply chains, not retail
  - similar survey in another reference
  - article on ChatGPT etc. as game changer for 21st century supply chain excellence; mainly language models, not DGM techniques in retail
  - review of 43 papers on deep learning in supply chain management; not exclusively DGMs or retail
  - survey of DGMs (Energy-based models, VAEs, GANs, Autoregressive models) + supply chain applications; not end-to-end, not retail, no insights for specific retail problems

- no existing survey on DGMs in retail supply chain -> we fill this gap (techniques + business usecases)
- contributions: (1) taxonomy/overview of DGMs and variants; (2) review of retail supply chain applications, end-to-end view; (3) insights and potential directions
- organization: Sec 2 DGM overview; Sec 3 purchase; Sec 4 logistics; Sec 5 sell; Sec 6 summary and conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Artificial intelligence is advancing fast, and in particular generative models are blossoming, which has started a new era for many fields and changed the way we perceive, interact and innovate with technology. This step is vital for keeping the supply chain efficient and effective. The last phase is sell, which is the actual sale and then the delivery of products to customers, and this completes the cycle from supplier to consumer.

Because the modern retail supply chain is so complex, many challenges come up in each phase, and this motivates researchers and practitioners to look for innovative solutions. For example, forecasting demand accurately is a long-existing challenge in the purchase phase, and it is often fraught with the unpredictability of consumer behavior and market conditions. On top of this, the supply chain has to be modeled and simulated to anticipate potential disruptions and bottlenecks. Creating accurate models is complex because there are many variables and stochastic elements in supply chain processes, and this needs advanced tools and methodologies. Another example is the optimality gap, which is the difference between the most efficient theoretical solution and the real-world execution, and it is a persistent issue. This gap can come from different factors, including but not limited to logistical stochasticity, supply chain end-to-end visibility, and computational NP-hardness. These discrepancies often cause inefficiencies that ripple through the supply chain and show up as delayed deliveries, increased carrying costs, and diminished service levels, so it is always impactful and valuable to develop advanced methods that improve optimality. So being able to adapt and optimize the end-to-end process is not just a competitive advantage but a survival imperative in the volatile landscape of global commerce.

With generative AI blossoming, some researchers have tried to give a survey or review of existing DGMs used in supply chain problems. Ooi et al gave a comprehensive discussion of the potentials of using DGMs across disciplines, including generative AI in retail. This work is timely and insightful, but it is more a high-level discussion of the potentials of DGMs in the supply chains of many areas, and it does not focus on the retail supply chain. A similar survey can also be found in another reference. Another article tries to address how DGM applications such as ChatGPT may be a game changer in 21st century supply chain excellence. That paper focuses on specific applications of DGMs, mainly language models, instead of discussing how to leverage techniques and methods of DGMs in the retail supply chain. Another reference aims to give a comprehensive vision by reviewing 43 papers on the applications of Deep Learning methods to supply chain management, trends, perspectives, and potential research gaps. It contains relevant insights on using deep learning in supply chain, but it does not focus only on DGMs or the retail supply chain. One more reference is a timely survey that briefly explains recent developments in DGMs, including Energy-based models, Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks, and Autoregressive models. It also reviews recent applications of these techniques to supply chain, but it does not discuss supply chain applications in an end-to-end way. This survey is a good starting point for practitioners to understand the landscape of DGMs, but it is not focused on the retail supply chain and it lacks insights on how DGMs can be applied to solve specific problems in the retail supply chain.

As far as we know, there is no other survey or review paper that focuses on the existing and potential applications of DGMs in the retail supply chain. This paper fills this gap by giving a comprehensive review of both the techniques and the business usecases of DGMs in the retail supply chain. Our contributions are:

- 1. We give a taxonomy and overview of state-of-the-art DGMs and their variants.

- 2. We review existing DGM applications in the retail supply chain from an end-to-end point of view.

- 3. We discuss insights and potential directions for how DGMs can be used further to solve retail supply chain problems.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section 2 gives a brief overview of DGMs with a taxonomy and introduces several popular models and their variants. Section 3 discusses applications of DGMs in the purchase phase. Section 4 is about applications of DGMs in the logistics phase. Section 5 is about applications of DGMs in the sell phase. And Section 6 summarizes the previous three sections and concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, specifically the blossoming of generative models, has ushered in a new era for diverse fields, fundamentally altering the way we perceive, interact, and innovate with technology. Tools like ChatGPT [1] and DALL-E [2] have shown the world their incredible power in generating content such as text or images.

The capability to generate human-like text, to understand context, and even to create artistic content was nothing short of revolutionary, and it brought people's attention to the science beneath these AI tools — Deep Generative Models (DGMs). Practitioners are taking action to leverage DGMs to pivot areas as diverse as healthcare [3], finance [4], entertainment, and more, in a storming way.

The retail supply chain is a key component of the modern economy, ensuring the smooth flow of goods from origin to end-users. In general, it can be segmented into three distinct phases: purchase, logistics, and sell [5,6]. The purchase phase entails the strategic acquisition of goods from vendors, a process driven by demand forecasting and procurement policies. Logistics, the second phase, involves transporting these goods from vendors to distribution centers (DCs), and then from DCs to retail outlets; this step is vital in maintaining the efficiency and effectiveness of the supply chain. The final phase, sell, encompasses the actual sale and subsequent delivery of products to customers, completing the cycle from supplier to consumer.

Due to the complexity of the modern retail supply chain, a host of challenges arise in each phase, motivating researchers and practitioners to seek innovative solutions. For example, forecasting demand accurately is a long-existing challenge in the purchase phase, often fraught with the unpredictability of consumer behavior and market conditions [7]. This challenge is compounded by the need to model and simulate the supply chain to anticipate potential disruptions and bottlenecks. Creating accurate models is complex because of the numerous variables and stochastic elements inherent in supply chain processes, which require advanced tools and methodologies [8,9]. As another instance, the optimality gap — the divergence between the most efficient theoretical solution and the real-world execution — poses a persistent issue. This gap can be attributed to various factors, including but not limited to logistical stochasticity, supply chain end-to-end visibility, and computational NP-hardness [10]. These discrepancies often lead to inefficiencies that ripple throughout the supply chain, manifesting in delayed deliveries, increased carrying costs, and diminished service levels [11,12], and therefore it is always impactful and valuable to develop advanced methods to improve optimality. As a result, the ability to adapt and optimize the end-to-end process is not just a competitive advantage but a survival imperative in the volatile landscape of global commerce.

With the blossoming of generative AI, some researchers have attempted to provide a survey or review of existing DGMs used in supply chain problems. Ooi et al provided a comprehensive discussion of the potentials of using DGMs across disciplines, including generative AI in retail [13]. This work is timely and insightful; however, it is more of a high-level discussion of the potentials of DGMs in many areas' supply chains, without focusing on the retail supply chain. A similar survey can also be found in reference [14]. Article [15] attempts to address how DGM applications such as ChatGPT may be a game changer in 21st century supply chain excellence. This paper focuses on specific applications of DGMs, mainly language models, rather than discussing how to leverage the techniques and methods of DGMs in the retail supply chain. Reference [16] aims to provide a comprehensive vision by reviewing 43 papers on the applications of Deep Learning methods to supply chain management, trends, perspectives, and potential research gaps. Although it contains relevant insights on leveraging deep learning in supply chain, it is not exclusively focused on DGMs or the retail supply chain. Reference [17] is a timely survey which briefly explains recent developments in DGMs, including Energy-based models, Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks, and Autoregressive models. It also reviews recent applications of these techniques to supply chain, although it does not discuss supply chain applications in an end-to-end way. This survey is a good starting point for practitioners to understand the landscape of DGMs; however, it is not focused on the retail supply chain and lacks insights on how DGMs can be applied to specific problems in the retail supply chain.

To the best of our knowledge, there is no other existing survey or review paper focusing on the existing and potential applications of DGMs in the retail supply chain. This paper fills this gap by providing a comprehensive review of both the techniques and the business usecases of DGMs in the retail supply chain. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

- 1. This paper provides a taxonomy and overview of state-of-the-art DGMs and their variants.

- 2. This paper reviews existing DGM applications in the retail supply chain from an end-to-end point of view.

- 3. This paper discusses insights and potential directions on how DGMs can be further utilized to solve retail supply chain problems.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a brief overview of DGMs with a taxonomy and introduces several popular models and their variants. Section 3 discusses the applications of DGMs in the purchase phase. Section 4 discusses the applications of DGMs in the logistics phase. Section 5 discusses the applications of DGMs in the sell phase. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the previous three sections and concludes the paper.
